newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic's hesitation muddies political crisis.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic's hesitation muddies political crisis.

text.p: President Slobodan Milosevic's reluctance to put his foot down has sown confusion in the Serbian political crisis but signs that he will retreat before opposition protesters are growing.
"In a country where the rule of law doesn't count for much, only the man at the top can enforce a decision on the way ahead and he has not played his cards in public yet," one Western diplomat said.

Milosevic's hesitation has blunted the impact of initial concessions to an opposition bloc that has protested in the streets for eight weeks over the annulment of Serbia-wide municipal elections lost by his Socialist Party (SPS).
A subsequent inquiry by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) confirmed the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition had won 14 of Serbia's 18 biggest towns.

OSCE findings backed SPS authorities into a corner and precipitated an uncoordinated scramble by various state bodies to defuse the pressure without giving away the store in the absence of Milosevic's explicit approval.

A Justice Ministry inquiry found Zajedno had indeed been cheated of victory in Serbia's second city Nis and ordered the outcome reinstated. But the hardline local SPS party machine has ignored the order and has not yet been pulled into line.
Calls by two deputy Serbian prime ministers and the SPS mayor of the capital Belgrade for "the will of the people to be fully respected" have not been fully answered yet.

On Tuesday, the Belgrade electoral commission said Zajedno had won a majority in the city assembly. It was a breakthrough but the commission cautioned the results were preliminary. This left room for appeals, reversals or other delays.
Throughout, Milosevic has remained conspicuously silent.
Analysts say he has temporised while authoritarian diehards and democratically-inclined moderates in his coterie have argued over a solution at several emergency meetings.
While they wrangled, Milosevic has brooded over his two options, neither pleasing.

He can concede to the sort of democratic groundswell that eventually voted out other leftist oligarchies in Eastern Europe, or resort to police force and risk ostracism by the West and economic collapse, if not a Romanian-style bloodbath.

Mindful of the parlous economy in Serbian-led federal Yugoslavia and uncertain about the loyalty of his police if ordered to crush peaceful protests, Milosevic chose on Friday to concede quietly, senior political sources say.
But he appeared to be still searching for ways to do so indirectly, without losing face, in his macho Balkan culture.
"It is the mother of all confusions. Decisions are being made and changed on a daily basis and no one really knows what to do (now)," a senior political source told Reuters on Monday.
But he and other sources contacted by Reuters and independent Belgrade newspapers said SPS moderates were winning the upper hand with Milosevic's blessing.

They said Milosevic convened a conclave of government ministers and senior officials of the SPS and allied Yugoslav United Left (JUL) party on Sunday night and it was again decided to restore the vote results. But how and when?

Electoral commissioners' hedging on the Belgrade results illustrates the problem. The Belgrade assembly is the grand prize in the voting, presiding over 20 percent of Serbia's population and controlling key media organs and legal bodies.
Losing large municipalities would also expose the SPS to investigations into serious corruption by party apparatchiks and managers of state enterprises.

Political sources said SPS hardliners persuaded Milosevic last weekend to stall an already-made decision to recognise the Zajedno victories after the Contact Group of Western powers and Russia said they would not impose sanctions on Serbia for now.

But Milosevic may also have been swayed by repeated Western warnings that Yugoslavia will be denied urgent financial aid and re-entry to international institutions like the World Bank unless it embarks on democratic reform.
Central Socialist authorities, however, would retain a strong hand even if Zajedno takes over municipal governments.

The federal government could make Zajedno look inept in advance of parliamentary and presidential elections later this year by holding up funding to and refusing to cooperate with opposition-led municipalities.
